issues.legal_issue: A personal extension of the limitation period available to one claimant does not revive another claimant’s time-barred rights.
material_facts: One claimant’s military service entitled him to an extended limitation period, a point that was not disputed.
The other claimant’s rights had already become time-barred, and he was transposed from defendant to plaintiff in the first appeal.
issues.conclusion: The extension was personal to the claimant entitled to it and could not benefit the other claimant; the suit therefore failed as to the latter’s share.
issues.legal_principle: A limitation privilege arising from a claimant’s personal disability is personal and does not revive another person’s barred rights.

predicates.suit_involves_multiple_claimants: More than one claimant seeks relief concerning rights in the same property.
predicates.one_claimant_has_personal_limitations_ex: One claimant has an extended limitation period because of a personal circumstance or disability.
predicates.another_claimant_right_is_time_barred: Another claimant’s right to sue has become time-barred.

issues.definition: When multiple claimants seek relief and only one has a personal limitation extension, that extension does not revive another claimant’s time-barred right.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant relying on customary law to challenge an alienation must prove that the disputed land itself was ancestral and devolved by inheritance.
material_facts: The claim to challenge the alienation under the applicable customary law depended on proving that the property was ancestral.

Settlement records connected a remote ancestor with the founding of a village and a share in one of its divisions, but did not establish the extent of that ancestor’s share or identify the disputed land as land he held.

Later records showed the family’s shares and landholdings, but did not establish that the specific holdings had descended from the remote ancestor; the recorded shares concerned jointly held village property, and the holdings were unequal.
The claimant produced no other evidence establishing that the disputed land had devolved by inheritance.
issues.conclusion: The claimant did not discharge the burden of proving that the disputed property was ancestral, so the claim failed.
issues.legal_principle: The burden rests on the claimant to establish the ancestral character of the land. Under the rule stated in Mt. Subbani v. Nawab and Imam Din v. Said Bibi, naming a common ancestor in a revenue pedigree is insufficient: it must also be proved that the descendants held the land in ancestral shares and that the land occupied at the time of the dispute devolved on them by inheritance.

predicates.customary_ancestral_property_claim: A claimant seeks to challenge an alienation under a customary rule that makes the claim depend on the property being ancestral.
predicates.remote_ancestor_link_only: The evidence links a remote ancestor to a community or territorial share but does not identify the disputed land as land held by that ancestor.
predicates.later_holdings_do_not_establish_inherite: Later records show family holdings but do not establish that those holdings descended from the remote ancestor by inheritance.
predicates.recorded_shares_do_not_show_the_disputed: Recorded shares concern jointly held property or otherwise do not establish that the specific disputed land descended by inheritance.

issues.definition: Where a customary ancestral-property claim rests only on a remote ancestral link and later records do not establish inherited continuity for the disputed land, the claimant fails to prove its ancestral character.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may examine the facts in a second appeal when the usual statutory restriction on factual review does not apply.
material_facts: The case reached the High Court in second appeal, where the High Court reconsidered the finding about whether the property was ancestral.
The usual statutory restriction on factual review in second appeals did not apply.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to examine the facts in second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code did not apply, so the High Court was entitled to go into the facts in second appeal.

predicates.proceeding_is_a_second_appeal: The matter is before a High Court as a second appeal.
predicates.usual_fact_review_restriction_is_inappli: The usual legal restriction limiting factual review in a second appeal does not apply to the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a matter is a second appeal and the usual restriction on factual review does not apply, the High Court may examine the facts.
